title: the Vijnana Bhairava (112 practices, one a day for 40 days)
hook: an empty room after moving day, and a jar worth staring into

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vijnana Bhairava let two voices talk about delight: guard the door, or walk through it with eyes open. Today, a door with nothing in it at all.

Moving day leaves a particular sound. Footsteps in a room with no rugs, no couch, no pictures: every step echoes. The eyes go hunting for something to land on and find only bare walls and the pale square where a frame used to hang. It's easy to hurry past a room like that. So why would a sacred book tell you to stop and stare into an empty jar? Because in the Vijnana Bhairava, the empty part is the point.
screen: `EVERY STEP ECHOES.` → `NOTHING TO LOOK AT.` → `STARE INTO THE JAR?`

segments.voice: Several of Bhairava's practices are built out of space, what Sanskrit calls akasha. One says: fix your gaze on the open sky, clear of clouds, without moving it, and let the mind take on the sky's stillness. Another takes a jar. Look at the space inside it, and leave the walls out of your attention. As the walls drop away, the text says, the mind dissolves into that space. A third turns inward: feel your own body as empty, like the sky. Notice the reversal. The walls are what anyone would call the jar. This practice says the part that holds the water is the part that's empty. And look at what space does. It holds the jar, the room, the clouds, everything you've ever seen, and none of it stains it. Things move through, and it doesn't move. In this text, that's a picture of awareness itself. An image that fits: a thought crosses the mind the way a bird crosses the sky, and the sky never chases the bird. So the practice isn't forcing the head empty. It's noticing the openness that was holding everything all along, even in a room full of boxes.
screen: `THE SKY, THE JAR, THE BODY.` · `THE EMPTY PART HOLDS THE WATER.` · `SPACE HOLDS ALL, STAINED BY NONE.` · then, large: `THE EMPTY PART HOLDS EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Pick up an empty cup or bowl, or any empty container near you. Feel its weight in your hands, then look into it: not at the rim or the walls, but at the space inside. Let your gaze go soft there, and when a thought comes, let it cross like a bird and come back to the open space in the cup. If there's no cup nearby, cup your two hands together and look into the space they hold.
The Vijnana Bhairava: a book of doors. Today's door is made of space: the sky, the jar, the openness that holds it all.
One line to keep: the Vijnana Bhairava, where the empty part holds everything. That's today.
